Jeudi matin, le Quartier chinois, d’ordi: On Thursday morning, Chinatown, usually bustling with life, was unusually deserted. A kind of tension hung in the air. The neighbourhood is once again at an impasse, cornered by speculators. Worry is growing over property buyers who threaten to wipe out this neighbourhood, whose footprint shrinks year after year.
<strong>« Si tout le monde commence à ac: “If everyone starts buying in Chinatown, there won’t be a Chinatown anymore!”
M. Yang, qui préfère taire son prénom, f: Mr. Yang, who prefers not to give his first name, is one of those who are outraged. He and his wife have owned Yiren Canada, a shop selling traditional Asian clothing, since 2013. He fears falling victim to the same fate as other buildings in Chinatown. “If outsiders buy my shop, of course that would be bad. If everyone starts buying in Chinatown, there won’t be a Chinatown anymore!” says the owner in his shop. “But I agree with people who are interested in investing in Chinatown to preserve the unique character of the area.”
Pour M. Yang, la préservation du Quartie: For Mr. Yang, preserving Chinatown is an existential question. Because his store sells traditional clothing, doing business in a non-Asian area is impossible for him, given the lack of customers.
Aux murs de son petit magasin est accroc: On the walls of his small store hangs his specialty: the qipao, a style of traditional Chinese dress often worn by women on special occasions. “My reputation goes beyond Montréal. I have plenty of customers who come from Toronto or Vancouver and tell me that in those cities, there’s no store like this,” says the shopkeeper, who immigrated to Quebec in 2001 with his children.Benny Y.W. Shek is the manager of the Kim Fung restaurant.
Pour lui, la cause de ce phénomène est é: For him, the cause of this phenomenon is economic. He is harsh toward Chinese investors who don’t see the neighbourhood’s value. “If the newly arrived Chinese investors wanted to improve Chinatown, it would become a much more interesting place,” he says. “But they don’t want to, and that keeps the neighbourhood from being at its best.”
Des investisseurs ont acheté la plus anc: Investors have bought the oldest part of Chinatown. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Dernièrement, l’achat de la partie la pl: Recently, the purchase of the oldest part of the neighbourhood sparked an outcry. The site, just one block from Mr. Yang’s business, was bought by Investissements 1000 Saint-Urbain. The Groupe de travail du Quartier chinois de Montréal issued a call for immediate action to protect this area, rich in the history of the French, Scottish, Jewish and Chinese communities that have passed through it. This latest development is part of a long series of real estate projects that have shrunk the neighbourhood over time.
L’embourgeoisement progressif du Quartie: The gradual gentrification of Chinatown has not gone unnoticed by Qing Shu, a mother. She has been a cashier at the Kim Fung restaurant since 2017. “It’s true that over the years, I’ve noticed that Chinatown has shrunk,” she confides. Alone in the big restaurant emptied out by COVID-19, she prepares takeout orders and barely has time to catch her breath.
Arrivée en 2002 au Québec, où l’attendai: She arrived in Quebec in 2002, where her husband, who had immigrated in the 1990s, was waiting for her. She first worked as a seamstress before turning to the restaurant business in 2010. Like many restaurant employees in Chinatown, who spend long hours at work and are not comfortable in French or English, she wasn’t really aware of the recent property purchase. Upon learning of it, the mother of two exclaims: “I think if outsiders buy Chinatown, we Chinese won’t have anywhere to go!”
Le Service de la famille chinoise du Gra: The Chinese Family Service of Greater Montréal is a support organization serving the Chinese diaspora. According to its executive director, Xixi Li, Ms. Shu’s profile is typical of recently arrived Chinese immigrants: economic immigrants in their thirties who were able to settle in Canada thanks to their university education, but who can’t find work in their field because of systemic racism that forces them to start from scratch. The Chinese Family Service of Greater Montréal is currently a tenant in one of the buildings that were bought.
À cause des nombreux problèmes structure: Because of the building’s many structural problems and the precariousness of being a tenant, Ms. Li had decided four years ago to move, well before the building was purchased. “We will be at 1088 Clark Street, a building we bought. It’s still in Chinatown, and our clients will be able to find us there.
On prévoit rester très longtemps à cette: We plan to stay at this address for a very long time,” says the woman who has worked at the Chinese Family Service for more than 20 years. The move nonetheless seems to sadden Xixi Li. She worries about the future of the neighbourhood, so rich in stories for Montréal’s Chinese diaspora, she confides in her office.
<strong>La longue histoire de l’exclusio: A long history of Chinese exclusion in real estate
Les bureaux du Service de la famille chi: The offices of the Chinese Family Service of Greater Montréal. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
La situation que décrit Mme Li, c’est au: The situation Ms. Li describes is also what many members of the Chinese diaspora who have lived in the neighbourhood for more than 50 years are going through. “The owners of commercial buildings can no longer afford it, they have to sell,” explains Winston Chan, a Chinese community leader. On top of repair costs, owners have to pay high municipal taxes and often struggle to make money from their property for lack of tenants.
M. Chan explique que, souvent, ne dispos: Mr. Chan explains that, often lacking sufficient income, they have to sell. “If the space is vacant, they have no money; they have to pay out of their own pocket just to remain owners of their building,” says Mr. Chan. The gradual destruction of Montréal’s Chinatown began in the 1950s, as downtown property values began to rise. Speculators took advantage to demolish buildings in the neighbourhood and replace them with parking lots. The shrinking continued.
De grands projets immobiliers ont réduit: Major real estate projects cut the neighbourhood’s footprint by a third in the 1970s. A school, two churches, several businesses, many homes and cultural associations were destroyed, despite the courageous resistance of the Chinese community at the time. According to Donny Seto, an urban planning professor at Concordia University and a Chinatown specialist, this failure can be explained by the government’s lack of transparency about its urban renewal plans and by communication and language barriers with a large part of the Chinese population.
Il croit que plusieurs facteurs ont fait: He believes several factors made Chinatown easy prey for real estate development. “In our culture, we don’t necessarily want to talk about our worries and our problems. We are very discreet people,” the professor explains.
Seto ajoute qu’aujourd’hui, les grands p: Seto adds that today, the large property owners around Chinatown are selling their housing to a wealthier population, which drives up the cost of neighbouring housing.
Selon May Chiu, membre du Groupe de trav: According to May Chiu, a member of the Groupe de travail du Quartier chinois and a lawyer by profession, the gentrification of Chinatown comes from the same source that has fuelled discrimination against the Chinese community since the start of the pandemic. In her view, the urban speculation and real estate development targeting Chinatown are symptoms of widespread systemic racism against Chinese people.
« Pourquoi est-ce qu’on ne peut pas cont: “Why can’t we control the land in Chinatown? Because we were victims of so many discriminatory laws!” says Ms. Chiu. “Because the dominant population thought we weren’t organized enough, they figured it would be easier to expropriate Chinatown to build on their land,” she believes. Despite all its resistance, the community did not have enough political power to prevent the expropriation of the neighbourhood. Community organizers ended up bargaining, asking for the construction of a community centre, social housing and a cultural centre.
Pour sauver ce quartier coloré, le Group: To save this colourful neighbourhood, the Groupe de travail sur le Quartier chinois de Montréal is asking the City of Montréal to designate it a “historic district.” This designation would protect the area’s buildings from destruction, a measure that saved a Chinese Catholic church in the 1970s. Thanks to this designation, Chinatown’s unique cultural heritage would be protected.
Ce statut vient toutefois avec plusieurs: However, this status comes with several constraints, according to Chinese community leaders. “I want it to be protected, but the owner has responsibilities, which complicates things,” says Winston Chan. He cites in particular the construction and maintenance work needed for heritage conservation. “It costs a lot, and there are owners who don’t have the money for that. The city needs to be able to help these owners,” he says. At the time of writing, the City of Montréal had not wished to comment on the matter.
Florence Yee, membre du groupe anti-embo: Florence Yee, a member of the Toronto anti-gentrification group Friends of Chinatown Toronto (FOCT), doesn’t think this measure serves the people. “I look at other Chinatowns that were able to get this status. It can be good for a community that no longer exists, where people no longer live,” says the activist, who believes a “historic district” designation designates a dead place. “[From a logistical standpoint], it means the buildings can’t change, can’t be renovated. It doesn’t protect the community, the people, the residents, the small businesses, all of which can be evicted and replaced.”
Le groupe de Florence Yee s’est tourné v: Florence Yee’s group has turned to a long-term, multi-pronged plan to protect Toronto’s Chinatown, for which heritage status was not sought. To address the inaccessibility of information about public consultations and the language barrier, Friends of Chinatown Toronto translated the information into simplified Chinese and produced posters to encourage people to participate across Toronto. FOCT also shared the information on Chinese social media, including WeChat. Thanks to these methods, instead of the usual 10 people, the group managed to bring 100 people to the first public consultation on a real estate project in Toronto.
FOCT a également tissé des liens étroits: FOCT has also built close ties with longtime local activists and urban planning experts. Thanks to these people, the group was able to research the median income of residents of Toronto’s Chinatown, which hovers around $28,000, very low for Toronto, as part of its demands for affordable housing in the area. It used this data to present municipal authorities with a definition of “affordable housing” more grounded in people’s reality than the one that had prevailed until then.
FOCT a eu du succès grâce à une équipe t: FOCT has succeeded thanks to a tight-knit team and systematic procedures for teaching new volunteer members who join the group. It also has <l1>a good number of direct action kits</l1> that people can use. “We really want to focus on the health of the community. Our super long-term project is to have a community land trust. [That means] the land where the building is acquired will be in the community permanently and will never go back on the market,” says Florence.
Ayant vécu à Montréal auparavant, Floren: Having lived in Montréal before, Florence believes Montréal’s Chinese activist groups could be more effective and improve their chances of success by building ties with other groups and developing a long-term strategy rather than reacting to problems as they arise.
Le Groupe de travail sur le Quartier chi: The Groupe de travail sur le Quartier chinois plans to adopt these strategies. It is looking for social media enthusiasts who can raise awareness on WeChat, Facebook and Instagram in Montréal. It also needs people who can design posters in French, English, simplified Chinese, traditional Chinese and Vietnamese. For her part, Ms. Chiu strongly encourages Chinese people to take part in the upcoming municipal elections.
« Les Chinois doivent participer, comme: “Chinese people have to participate, like all the other communities, and ask candidates what they propose to protect Chinatown, to fight gentrification, to make sure there are more services and to protect residents,” she says.
Le professeur Seto, lui, voit une soluti: Professor Seto sees a potential solution in the future of urban planning.
La semaine passée, ses étudiants en urba: Last week, his urban planning students presented urban design plans for Chinatown that preserve the area’s heritage and allow the people who live, work and spend time there to have a good quality of life. These up-and-coming planners have already sent their plans to the City of Montréal.
Yang, quant à lui, ne veut surtout pas q: Yang, for his part, above all doesn’t want the neighbourhood to lose its heritage. “If my shop gets bought and I’m forbidden to reopen it, I’ll be super disappointed. I think all the small shopkeepers in the neighbourhood would be disappointed!” he exclaims with sadness and frustration. “We would lose the character and the culture of this neighbourhood. As long as Chinatown exists, people will know this neighbourhood exists and will enjoy beautiful things here.”
